name: MathQA
description: A large-scale dataset of 37,200 math word problems with operation-based formal annotations. The dataset enhances the AQuA dataset by providing fully-specified operational programs for solving math word problems across multiple domains including geometry, physics, probability, gain-loss, and general mathematics.

creator.name: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
creator.affiliation: University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI

citeAs: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi. 2019. MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319v1 [cs.CL]
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by taking math word problems from the AQuA dataset and annotating them with formal operation programs using crowdsourcing. Problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies, then annotated through a dynamic annotation platform.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source is the AQuA-RAT dataset, which provides over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level math word problems. The dataset consists of multiple-choice math word problems from a wide range of domains.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Problems from AQuA were filtered for solvability. Unsolvable problems were removed, including those with no words (37 problems), sequence problems (1,991 problems), problems requiring options enumeration (6,643 problems), non-numeric problems (10,227 problems), and duplicates (17,294 problems). From 97,467 total AQuA training problems, 65,991 were identified as solvable. Annotation expansion was performed by finding closely similar problems using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance, replacing numeric values with generic numbers.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Math problems were categorized into domains (Geometry, Physics, Probability, Gain-Loss, General, Other) using term frequencies. A lexicon of n-grams relating to specific domains was constructed. For each domain category, associated n-grams that occur frequently in that domain but rarely in others were selected. Problems were assigned category labels based on highest n-gram frequency.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators used a dynamic annotation platform to sequentially select operations and arguments until problems were solved. The platform provided: (a) basic math knowledge through operation hints with arguments, formulas, and explanations, (b) dynamic calculation of intermediate results after each operation submission, and (c) quality control through test questions. Annotators selected operations from category-specific lists, then chose arguments from valid options (numbers in problem, constants, previous calculations). Programs were only accepted if they included numbers from the problem and final calculations matched the correct numeric solution within a threshold. At least 2 out of 3 validators had to rank an operation program as valid for selection.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Validation accuracy was 94.64% across categories. Expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% of annotations were valid, with 87% agreement between expert validation and crowdsourcing validation tasks.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each problem received annotations from multiple annotators, with at least 2 out of 3 validators required to approve each operation program.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: An automatic dynamic programming approach was experimented with to generate operation programs using numbers in AQuA rationales, but only 61% passed human validation due to incomplete rationales. These automatic annotations were not included in the final dataset to maintain interpretability.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset inherits some characteristics from AQuA, including near-duplicate problems with slight changes to stories or numerical values. The categorization strategy may introduce noise due to using only one mathematical interpretation for each domain-specific n-gram (e.g., 'square' or 'cube' can refer to geometry or exponential operations). Agreement between human annotators on categorization was 84%, with 74.5% agreement between humans and the automated categorization model.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset does not cover all types of math problems. Limitations include: (1) High-order polynomials are omitted, (2) Problems with entirely non-numeric solutions are excluded, (3) Sequence problems requiring pattern understanding are currently unsolvable, (4) Some problems require complicated or long chains of mathematical reasoning beyond current model capabilities, (5) Some mathematical operations like factorization are not defined in the representation language, (6) Problems solvable only by brute-force enumeration rather than logical reasoning are excluded. Analysis of 50 incorrectly solved problems showed error categories: hard problems requiring complex reasoning (45%), limitations in representation language (25%), categorization errors (12.5%), and incorrect or insufficient problem text (17.5%).
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating neural models for math word problem solving. It is split into 80% training, 12% development, and 8% test sets. The dataset aims to improve both performance and interpretability of learned models through operation-based formalisms. Use cases include: (1) Training sequence-to-program models for math problem solving, (2) Evaluating interpretable AI systems, (3) Testing domain-aware categorization approaches, (4) Benchmarking logical reasoning capabilities of neural networks.
